lead: A dielectric is an insulator with no free charge to give. Put it between charged plates and its molecules stretch or turn into tiny dipoles. That polarization leaves bound charge on the faces, weakens the field inside by the factor ε_r, and raises the capacitance by the same factor. Ceramic capacitors in a phone charger and plastic film capacitors in a fan regulator both work this way.
prereq: You need Chapter 3.3 for Gauss's law, and Chapter 3.4 for potential and stored energy.

blocks.text: A dielectric is an insulator. Its electrons stay bound to their molecules, so it cannot supply charge to a circuit. It can only shift charge a little within each molecule, and that shift changes the field.

A nonpolar molecule has its centre of positive charge on top of its centre of negative charge, so it has no dipole moment of its own. Hydrogen, carbon dioxide and methane are examples. An applied field pulls the electrons one way and the nuclei the other, creating an induced dipole. Its moment is p = αE, where p is the dipole moment in C·m, α is the molecular polarizability in C·m²/V, and E is the field in V/m. Remove the field and the dipole disappears.

A polar molecule already has its charge centres apart. Water has a permanent dipole moment of 1.85 D, where 1 debye = 3.336×10⁻³⁰ C·m. With no field, thermal motion points the molecules in all directions and the net moment is zero. An applied field exerts a torque and turns them partly into line. Alignment is never complete, because thermal agitation keeps knocking them back.

One vector describes both effects. Polarization P is the total dipole moment per unit volume, in C/m². If there are N molecules per cubic metre each with average moment p, then P = Np. In a small field P = ε₀χ_eE, where χ_e is the electric susceptibility, a pure number, and ε₀ = 8.854×10⁻¹² F/m.

sections.h3: Bound charge and the displacement D

blocks.text: Polarization pushes charge to the surfaces. At a face where the dipoles point outwards, their positive ends stick out. The bound surface charge density there is σ_b = P·n̂, where n̂ is the outward unit normal and σ_b is in C/m². If P varies from place to place, charge also piles up inside with density ρ_b = −∇·P. This bound charge cannot be drained with a wire; it exists only while P exists.

Take two large plates carrying free charge density +σ and −σ. In vacuum the field is E₀ = σ/ε₀. Slide a slab between them and the bound charge on its faces opposes the plates. The field inside becomes E = (σ − σ_b)/ε₀, which works out to E = E₀/ε_r. The dielectric always weakens the field, never reverses it.

blocks.where: D is the electric displacement in C/m²; E is the field in V/m; P is the polarization in C/m²; Q_free is the charge you put on the plates, ignoring bound charge; ρ_free is the free volume charge density in C/m³.

blocks.text: D is bookkeeping. Its flux out of a closed surface counts only free charge, so for a given plate charge D is the same with or without the slab. For a linear dielectric, D = ε₀(1 + χ_e)E = ε₀ε_rE, with ε_r = 1 + χ_e the relative permittivity. The older name dielectric constant, K, means the same number. Vacuum has χ_e = 0 and ε_r = 1.

sections.h3: Capacitors and the two battery cases

blocks.text: A capacitor is two conductors holding charges +Q and −Q at a potential difference V. Its capacitance is C = Q/V, in farad, where 1 F = 1 C/V. For parallel plates of area A and separation d with vacuum between, C₀ = ε₀A/d. Fill the gap with a dielectric of relative permittivity ε_r and C = ε₀ε_rA/d = ε_rC₀.
Capacitors in series share the same Q and add voltages: 1/C = 1/C₁ + 1/C₂ + …. Capacitors in parallel share the same V and add charge: C = C₁ + C₂ + ….
U = ½CV² = Q²/2C = ½QV,   u = ½ε₀ε_rE²
blocks.where: U is the stored energy in joule; C is the capacitance in farad; V is the potential difference in volt; Q is the charge in coulomb; u is the energy density in J/m³; E is the field in the dielectric in V/m.

blocks.text: Now the two cases. With the battery still connected, V is fixed. Inserting the slab raises C by ε_r, so Q = CV rises by ε_r, E = V/d stays the same, and U rises by ε_r; the battery supplies the extra charge. With the battery removed, Q is fixed. C rises by ε_r, so V = Q/C falls to V₀/ε_r, E falls to E₀/ε_r, and U falls to U₀/ε_r. The lost energy went into pulling the slab into the gap — the field does mechanical work on it.

Every dielectric breaks down above some field. That limit is the dielectric strength, in V/m: about 3×10⁶ V/m for air at ordinary pressure, and several times more for mica or ceramic. Breakdown ionizes a path and a spark discharges the capacitor, so the plate separation must satisfy V < E_strength × d.

figure.caption: Free charge on the plates turns the molecules into dipoles; the bound charge they leave on the faces is what makes D depend only on the free charge and lifts the capacitance to ε_rC₀.

spec.title: What a dielectric does
spec.aria: Free charge on the plates lines up molecular dipoles, which leave bound charge on the faces, so D depends on free charge and the capacitance rises by the factor ε_r.

examples.question: A parallel plate capacitor has plate area A = 0.02 m² and separation d = 1 mm. Mica of relative permittivity ε_r = 5 fills the gap, and a battery keeps V = 100 V across the plates. Find (a) the vacuum capacitance C₀, (b) the capacitance C with mica, (c) the free charge Q on each plate, (d) the field E in the mica, (e) the stored energy U, and (f) the bound surface charge density σ_b.
steps: Vacuum capacitance: C₀ = ε₀A/d = (8.854×10⁻¹² × 0.02)/(1×10⁻³) = 1.77×10⁻¹⁰ F = 177 pF.
With mica: C = ε_rC₀ = 5 × 1.77×10⁻¹⁰ = 8.85×10⁻¹⁰ F = 885 pF.
Battery connected, so V is held at 100 V: Q = CV = 8.85×10⁻¹⁰ × 100 = 8.85×10⁻⁸ C.
Field: E = V/d = 100/(1×10⁻³) = 1.0×10⁵ V/m. Check with free charge: σ_free = Q/A = 8.85×10⁻⁸/0.02 = 4.43×10⁻⁶ C/m², and E = σ_free/(ε₀ε_r) = 4.43×10⁻⁶/(8.854×10⁻¹² × 5) = 1.0×10⁵ V/m.
Bound charge: σ_b = σ_free(1 − 1/ε_r) = 4.43×10⁻⁶ × (1 − 0.2) = 3.54×10⁻⁶ C/m², of opposite sign to the free charge on each face.
examples.check:
eps0 = 8.854e-12
A = 0.02
d = 1e-3
er = 5
V = 100
C0 = eps0 * A / d
C = er * C0
Q = C * V
E = V / d
U = 0.5 * C * V**2
sigma_free = Q / A
sigma_b = sigma_free * (1 - 1 / er)
print(C0)
print(C)
print(Q)
print(E)
print(U)
print(sigma_free)
print(sigma_b)

traps: Mixing up the two battery cases. With the battery connected V and E stay fixed and Q grows by ε_r; with the battery removed Q stays fixed and E and V fall to 1/ε_r.
Treating D and E as the same thing. D = ε₀ε_rE depends only on free charge for a given geometry; E is weakened by the bound charge. Their units differ too: C/m² against V/m.
Getting the sign of σ_b wrong. The bound charge is positive on the face where P points out of the dielectric, so it opposes the free charge on the plate it touches.
Using C = ε_rC₀ when the slab fills only part of the gap. That formula needs the whole gap filled; a partial slab is a dielectric and an air capacitor in series.

quiz.q: Define electric polarization P and give its SI unit.
quiz.a: P is the total dipole moment per unit volume of the dielectric. Unit: C/m².

quiz.q: Write the relation between D, E and P, and state Gauss's law for D.
quiz.a: D = ε₀E + P. The flux of D out of any closed surface equals the free charge enclosed: ∮D·dA = Q_free, or ∇·D = ρ_free.

quiz.q: Why are polar molecules only partly aligned by an applied field, while induced dipoles in nonpolar molecules appear fully?
quiz.a: Alignment of permanent dipoles competes with thermal motion, which randomizes directions, so only a fraction line up. An induced dipole is created by the field itself and is proportional to E at every instant, so it vanishes exactly when E vanishes.

quiz.q: An air capacitor of 200 pF is filled with mica of ε_r = 5 and connected to 50 V. Find the new capacitance and the charge on the plates.
A 2 μF and a 3 μF capacitor are joined in series across 100 V. Find the equivalent capacitance and the charge on each.
quiz.a: 1/C = 1/2 + 1/3 = 5/6 μF⁻¹, so C = 1.2 μF. Series capacitors share the same charge: Q = CV = 1.2×10⁻⁶ × 100 = 1.2×10⁻⁴ C on each.

quiz.q: A charged capacitor is disconnected from its battery and a dielectric slab is then inserted. Explain what happens to Q, V, E and U, and where the energy goes.
quiz.a: Q is fixed because the plates are isolated. C rises to ε_rC₀, so V = Q/C falls to V₀/ε_r and E falls to E₀/ε_r. U = Q²/2C falls to U₀/ε_r. The field pulls the slab in and does mechanical work equal to the drop in stored energy.

quiz.q: A dielectric slab weakens the field between the plates. Why does the field not become zero?
quiz.a: The bound charge is always smaller than the free charge, σ_b = σ_free(1 − 1/ε_r), so it only cancels part of the field. Complete cancellation would need ε_r infinite.

quiz.q: Why does D stay the same when a slab is inserted with the battery disconnected, while E changes?
quiz.a: D depends only on free charge through ∮D·dA = Q_free, and Q_free is unchanged, so D = σ_free is fixed. E = D/(ε₀ε_r) then drops by ε_r because the bound charge adds to the net charge in the ordinary Gauss law for E.

beyond: Not for the exam. Real capacitors use ceramics such as barium titanate, polymer films, aluminium oxide and tantalum oxide, chosen for high ε_r, high dielectric strength and stable behaviour with temperature. The gate insulator of a MOSFET is the same physics: silicon dioxide, now often replaced by hafnium oxide, sets how much charge the channel can hold. Search for 'high-k dielectric' and 'dielectric loss tangent' to go further.
